newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Long road ahead on Yugo debt deal, analysts.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Long road ahead on Yugo debt deal, analysts.

text.p: Yugoslavia's hopes of 80 percent debt forgiveness are highly unlikely to satisfy the London Club of commercial bank creditors and the two sides appear far from hammering out a deal any time soon, analysts said on Wednesday.
A Yugoslav delegation, which presented a proposal to its creditors to restructure $2.4 billion of debt, left London on Wednesday following two days of inconclusive talks.

"They had before claimed they would never ask for forgiveness and now they have come out with terms that are going to be completely unacceptable to creditors so we see ahead of us a long period of negotiations," said Susanne Hallegard, economist for Eastern Europe at ING Barings in London.

According to documents obtained by Reuters on Tuesday, Yugoslavia had asked commercial bank creditors for 80 percent forgiveness on $2.4 billion of debt and for a nine-year grace period before repayment begins. Under the current proposal outlined in the documents, Yugoslavia is seeking to issue $481 million via a syndicated loan with a 25-year maturity.

Yugoslavia's deputy Prime Minister Danko Djunic, who led the delegation, told Reuters on Tuesday he was open to further discussion with the banks but he did not believe the country would be able to repay more than 20 percent of total debt owed.
"We don't think we can possibly repay more than what we have offered," Djunic said.
Djunic did say though that he was flexible on the type of financial instrument used in debt restructuring.
However, at the same time, a banking source close to the talks said current terms of the debt restructuring proposal were no basis for negotiations.
Analysts agreed the stringent terms currently proposed by Yugoslavia to the London Club of commercial bank creditors would never be approved by the banks.

"We are looking at deals in other countries as some sort of potential benchmark and they (Yugoslavia) came in asking for a lot more which means it will take some time before this deal is done," said Ingrid Iverson, emerging market debt strategist at UBS Securities in London.
"The proposal is looking for a much bigger level of forgiveness than the banks had expected," she added.
Hallergard of ING agreed: "They would have to come to a compromise--25 years, 9 years grace and 80 percent forgiveness are just terms that the London Club would never accept."

Another factor likely to prolong Yugoslavia's debt restructuring with creditors is the fact that the country is not yet a member of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and analysts do not expect the country to gain membership this year.
"It (IMF membership) is being considered but it is unlikely to come until next year," said Iverson.
Djunic told Reuters after a news conference on Wednesday that he hoped for IMF membership by year-end.
IMF membership is not a precondition for a London Club agreement but analysts said Yugoslavia would never be able to service its debt without a standby agreement from the IMF.

"IMF membership is not a condition for the London Club agreement to be finalised but it is indirectly because Serbia would never be able to service its debt if it does not get some kind of standby loan from the IMF and...it doesn't look likely this year," said Hallegard.

While an agreement of 80 percent debt reduction appears unlikely, one economist suggested 50 percent forgiveness was far more feasible because the country would not be able to service more than that amount given the current state of its economy.

"I think it is positioning. The Yugoslavs are saying what can we get away with and the banks know they will not get 100 percent and we reckon a deal will be struck at around 50 percent," said David McWilliams, emerging markets strategist at Banque National de Paris in London.
"Without debt forgiveness it would be virtually impossible for Serbia to recover in a manifest way," he added.
